By coercing unknown methods to `_OTHER` (and `HTTP` for span names), the instrumentation now converts valid, non-standard HTTP request methods (like `PROPFIND` or `PURGE`) to `_OTHER`. The OpenTelemetry HTTP semantic conventions for [`http.request.method`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.37.0/docs/registry/attributes/http.md) mandate:
> "If the HTTP instrumentation could end up converting valid HTTP request methods to `_OTHER`, then it **MUST provide a way to override the list of known HTTP methods.** If this override is done via environment variable, then the environment variable **MUST be named `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_HTTP_KNOWN_METHODS`**..."

This PR introduces the fallback to `_OTHER` but fails to implement the required `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_HTTP_KNOWN_METHODS` environment variable override. Without this, consumers have no way to whitelist their valid custom methods, resulting in them being irreversibly masked as `_OTHER` and their span names mangled to `HTTP`.

This still uses a hardcoded `switch` block that duplicates the exact same keys present in `MethodLookup`. This is an unnecessary risk for drift (e.g., if a new method is added to the map but forgotten in the switch). Let's use the same lookup method as `requestMethodAttrs` here.

A matched literal nested inside another matched literal's `wrap`-ed field is silently skipped — including its own `value`-set fields — with no error or warning.

`matched` is collected once via a single top-down `dst.Inspect` pass before any mutation runs (lines 26-36), so it lists parents before their nested literals. When a parent's field is wrapped, `compileExpression` splices the *original* subtree into the template placeholder and the result is `dst.Clone`d (line 166) — a deep copy that installs a brand-new subtree in the tree. Any nested literal already captured in `matched` now points at an orphan: the loop still "mutates" it, but the mutation lands on a node the tree no longer contains.

Confirmed through the golden-test pipeline (rule wraps `R`, sets `N` on `io.LimitedReader`):

Input:
```go
&io.LimitedReader{R: &io.LimitedReader{R: base, N: 5}, N: 10}
```
Compiles to:
```go
&io.LimitedReader{R: counting(&io.LimitedReader{R: base, N: 5}), N: 99}
```

The outer literal is instrumented correctly; the inner one is completely untouched and the build succeeds silently. This is an ordinary reader/handler wrapper-chain shape, not a contrived case.

`recordTokenUsage` only emits a data point when the count is `> 0`, so a response
with genuinely zero tokens of a type (or a response body that omits `usage`
entirely) produces the same observable result: no data point at all. That's fine
for histogram *sums*, but it means the data point *count* for
`gen_ai.client.token.usage` can't be used to infer "how many operations had usage
data" — zero-usage and missing-usage are indistinguishable downstream.

Is skipping on zero intentional (e.g. to avoid noise from embeddings' always-zero
output side), or should this record `0` whenever the field was actually present
in the response? If it's the former, worth a one-line comment here saying so
explicitly, since the current comment above `recordTokenUsage` doesn't call out
the zero-skip as deliberate.

The PR description says token usage is recorded "in the streaming reader once
the stream finishes," but this branch never calls `recordTokenUsage` — the
streaming reader only sets span attributes (via the `streaming` package),
and `newStreamingReader` isn't given the histogram or `baseAttrs` at all.
`TestOtelMiddleware_StreamingResponse` confirms this: it asserts the
`gen_ai.usage.*` span attributes from a stream with a `usage` block, but never
checks the `gen_ai.client.token.usage` metric.

Since streaming is a common path for chat completions, this means token usage
goes unreported for a large share of real traffic. Either wire token recording
into the streaming finish path (mirroring how `gen_ai.usage.*` span attributes
are already set there), or update the PR description to say streaming is out
of scope for this change.

And there is already in-repo precedent for sharing across the three versions: `internal/streaming` is its own module, consumed by all three via `replace` directives:

```
openai-go/go.mod:74     => ./internal/streaming
openai-go/v2/go.mod:74  => ../internal/streaming

```

Anthropic reasonably stays separate, since it is a different vendor tree with no dependency on the openai internal module.

The `default` branch treats both 80 and 443 as default, which is a different rule from the two scheme-specific cases — under `https` a port of 80 is *not* default, and under `http` 443 is not.
